chapter_theme: Natrinai 21 to 40: short poems across the five lands, the friend's voice above all; she presses the man to marry, pleads his case to the girl, mocks the god called to the veri and the husband who denies his women, and reports the girl's tears; men going for wealth and returning, a mother whose daughter has gone with her lover, a courtesan jeering at the husband's midnight visit to his son, with Korkai, Maranthai, Koodal and Kaandavaayil as measures of beauty and home.

21.reading: Returning with his work done, the man tells his charioteer to let the weary attendants loosen their tight girdles and come on slowly at their own pace, and to use the goad he has never had to use and drive on, and bids him look at the forest cock, its throat speckled like milk sprinkled on melted ghee, which on the wide scrubland the rains have left scratches up the wet sand for its morning food and stands looking to its hen.
21.nuance: The man is easy on his tired men while hurrying himself, and he gives the poem's last words, 'noble bearing' (பெருந்தகு நிலை), to the bird, not to himself: his longing for his wife is shown only through what he points the charioteer to.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest cock on the rain-washed scrubland and the hero's homecoming fix mullai

comparisons.tenor: the speckles on the cock's throat

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (வலவ, line 5)

iraicchi.act: the cock scratches up the wet sand for the day's food and, having caught it, stands looking to its hen
iraicchi.sense: the man's own errand of provision is done and, like the fowl, he turns to the wife he provides for

22.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man has come, the lord of the land where a female monkey, taking the first-ripened heavy heads of the millet a hill girl guards, climbs the rock with her untaught mate and, crushing them in her palms and stuffing her cheeks, looks like rain-soaked ascetics eating from their hands; his coming is like rain pouring at midnight on paddy shrivelled in its sheath in a dry season when the ponds have lost their water.
22.nuance: The rain is timed to the last moment: it falls on paddy already shrivelled, at midnight when no one looks for it. The monkey who steals the guarded millet's first heads with her mate is a near miss for ullurai (only one pair, the guarded crop to the guarded girl, maps cleanly), so it is scene and simile here.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl's millet and the monkeys of the rock fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the female monkey crouched with millet in her cheeks and her back wet with rain
the man's coming to marry her

23.reading: Pressing the man to marry, the friend says the girl's shoulders escaped blame because her bangles hid their thinness, and her loosened hair has the excuse of play with her companions, but her eyes, which besides weeping each time they see the old beauty her mother watches over wasting away, have faded like the small-leaved neythal flower in the clear water of Korkai's pearl-bearing harbour, cannot hide love.
23.nuance: The friend sorts the signs into those an excuse can cover (bangles, hair) and the one that cannot (the eyes); line 3 (இடிப்பு மெய்யது ஒன்று உடைத்தே) is hard, and the hair's excuse is my reading of it.

colophon.thurai: தலைவி துயர் ஆற்றாமை உணர்ந்த தோழி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's only native things are of the Korkai shore, and its situation is the girl's grief that cannot be hidden

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which have lost their brightness

24.reading: The woman tells her friend, who said 'good' when the man said they would go to the hard tract of a strange land, where wood-apple trees, their trunks rough as if monitor lizards clung to them, drop fruit like balls left after play, their stalks snapped, onto green creepers spread like a blanket, and wood-apple is the only food, that she did well: men whose minds are set on action leave for the wealth to be made, and that is their nature.
24.nuance: The colophon says she speaks with joy, and the maxim is given as approval; set beside the many parting poems in which the woman refuses, the praise may also be read as bitter, and the poem does not settle which.

colophon.thurai: பொருட்பிரிவுக்கு உடன்பட்ட தோழியைத் தலைவி உவந்து கூறியது

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going for wealth across a hard tract is pirithal

comparisons.tenor: the rough-barked trunk of the wood-apple
the fallen wood-apple fruit
the green creepers spread on the ground

25.reading: Pleading the man's case, the friend tells the girl that the lord of the rich hill, where a bee dusted with the fragrant pollen of the pidavu, whose red-veined petals look like lac drawn on the back of a conch bangle, takes on the colour of a touchstone rubbed with gold, chased the parrots from the millet with them yesterday and, finding no chance to speak, went away; his going is not sorrow but love, and having seen his unwearied gaze, like a bee that, craving pollen, does not pick among the buds, she now thinks of her own graceless act of pressing back her slipping bangle.
25.nuance: The friend speaks as if the man's silent plea and her own refusal (the bangle pressed back) were hers, which lets her press his case without naming the girl's feelings; whether the 'graceless act' is the friend's or the girl's is not certain from the Tamil.

thinai_evidence.note: chasing parrots from the hill millet is the kurinji courtship scene

comparisons.tenor: the red-veined petals of the pidavu
the bee dusted with pollen
the man's unwearied gaze

26.reading: To keep the man from going, the friend asks: shall I grieve? her bangles have slipped; would it be a wrong if she, of the sharp white teeth, the gold-like spots, the full dark hair and broad shoulders, left her mother's house, with its tall granary of paddy, white-based and spotted, like a hill, to be your companion, even one who perishes, on the dry tract where under the full sun the jackfruit shrivels on the bent old tree?
26.nuance: The friend stops the journey by offering the girl as a fellow traveller, which the man must refuse; the rich granary of the mother's house is set against the shrivelled fruit of the road. Line 7 (கெடு துணை ஆகிய தவறோ) can also mean 'is it her fault that she has become a lost companion', and I cannot fix which.

colophon.thurai: தலைவி பிரிவு உணர்ந்து வேறுபட்டமை சொல்லி தோழி செலவு அழுங்குவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going across the sun-burnt tract is pirithal

comparisons.tenor: the tall granary of the mother's house
the spots on her skin

27.reading: With the man listening nearby, the friend tells the girl that yesterday they only played in the grove by the backwater, on the white sand the waves had lined, chasing off the bees that sprinkle fine pollen, and did nothing in secret, or if they did, no one else knew; so what did mother mean when she said, 'do not go and pluck the small-leaved neythal that, on long stems by the backwaters where the herons cry in flocks and sharks come, has bloomed like eyes'?
27.nuance: The mother's ban on picking flowers is the girl's confinement told sideways, so that the man overhearing learns the meetings are over; the reversed simile (flowers like eyes) puts watching eyes on every stem.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove, its herons, sharks and neythal fix the shore

comparisons.tenor: the neythal flowers

28.reading: The speaker says that the lord of the high-ridged hill, where falls drop like gems, the vengai spreads like gold over the slopes and swaying green bamboo rises to tear the running clouds, took her hand and pressed it to his eyes, stroked her brow with his own hand and spoke sweetly like a mother, yet he is cruel as thieves.
28.nuance: The two similes are set against each other in successive lines: like a mother, like thieves; the man's tender acts are the evidence for his cruelty, since they are what make his absence hurt.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண் ஆற்றாளாகிய தலைவிக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது - குறை நயப்பும் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the poem has only hill things; separation is implied only by 'cruel'

comparisons.tenor: his sweet words
the man, cruel after his tenderness
the falling water
the spread vengai blossom

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: on this reading the friend tells how the man courted her, to press his case

29.reading: The mother whose daughter has gone with her lover asks how the girl can manage the narrow grassy track where, in the lingering summer, the kanthal has withered, the long blazing stretch gives no shade, and a tiger, its mate starving after giving birth, waits in the dim evening to kill travellers, when at home, if her mother merely loosened her embrace for fear of hurting her young breasts, she would weep from her large rain-dark eyes and sigh hotly, that gentle girl of dark hair and great innocence.
29.nuance: The tiger hunting for its starving mate is a male providing for its mate, but striking its lines leaves the mother's question with no road to ask about, so it fails the deletion test and stays scene; the poem's weight is the contrast between a loosened hug and the tiger's track.

thinai_evidence.note: summer heat, shadelessness and the tiger on the track fix paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the mother speaks to those about her

30.reading: To the husband who says he knows no other woman, the friend says she has seen it, and what can she do: on the fine street where his bard's little lute hums like bees, the decked women who had laid claim to his chest stood watching for him to pass, and like the many who, when the ship capsizes in a gale, cling together to one plank with hot tears falling, they pull him this way and that in endless distress.
30.nuance: The shipwreck makes the man a plank, one object many lives cling to, so the friend's mockery deflates both his denial and his importance; the bard's lute, which announces his coming, is what gives him away.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைவன் யாரையும் அறியேன் என்றார்க்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the friend confronts the husband over the other women: oodal

comparisons.tenor: the hum of the bard's lute

comparisons.vehicle: கடல்மரம் கவிழ்ந்தெனக் கலங்கி உடன் வீழ்பு பலர் கொள் பலகை போல
comparisons.tenor: the women fighting over the man

31.reading: With the man standing nearby, the girl answers her friend's reassurance: the shore of small-flowered njaazhal, where a little white sea crow, having struck a red prawn after scanning the wide dark water, searches the cold backwater and calls to the mate it loves, would be sweet to her too, were she not grieving, thinking many things with a lonely heart, until she is married to the lord of the strong-watered shore, where goods brought by the wind from many lands are unloaded on the moonlit sand and a heavy-bellied white heron on the long-branched punnai fears the roaming tide.
31.nuance: The pregnant heron that fears the tide is close to the girl's own fear, but only that one pair maps, so it is scene. Line 5 recurs as Natrinai 311 line 7.

colophon.thurai: தலைவன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தலைவி வன்புறை எதிர் அழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, punnai, heron and the lord of the shore fix neythal

iraicchi.act: the male sea crow, having caught a red prawn, searches the backwater and calls the mate it loves to share it
iraicchi.sense: even the shore bird provides for and calls its mate, while the man has not yet married the girl

32.reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the hill, whose great slope is dark like Mayon and whose falls are bright white like Valiyon, desires them and has long suffered, yet she will not trust that true word: let her see him herself, weigh it with her people, learn his mind and judge, since once accepted it is hard to undo; the great take a friend only after inquiry, and do not inquire after they have befriended.
32.nuance: The closing maxim belongs to friendship (நட்பு), and the friend uses it in both directions at once: inquire, because once he is accepted there is no going back; the dark god and the white god give the hill its colours before any argument begins.

thinai_evidence.note: the great hill and its falls fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the dark slope of the great hill
the bright white waterfall

33.reading: The friend tells the man that the girl, sobbing, looked into her face and said 'if he means to cross the fearful path where, when the setting sun reaches the cleft hills and evening spreads over the hamlet on the gravel, by the dreary common where loneliness feeds, in hills that have never known full rain, where muddy water is drawn from stony pits, bowmen in dyed cloth with arrows on the string lie in wait for travellers, could we, soft as we are, stop him?', and her flower-like eyes brimmed and overflowed onto her breasts.
33.nuance: The friend reports the girl's words rather than pleading herself, so the girl's question (could we stop him?) reaches him as a fact already decided: she has not asked him to stay, only wept.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தலைமகளது குறிப்பு அறிந்த தோழி தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the man's intended crossing of the bandit path is pirithal

comparisons.tenor: her eyes

34.reading: Speaking as if to the god, the friend tells Murugan that the heavy lovesickness was given by the chest of the lord of the land where a nymph, wearing a garland of the unplucked blue lilies of the god's rock spring and blood-bright kanthal, dances to the sweet music of the falls on the great slope; knowing it is not his seizure, he still came, wearing a kadampu garland, to the veri house at the velan's call: god he may be, but he is surely a fool.
34.nuance: The friend's speech to the god is meant for the household, which has called the velan; by telling Murugan he knows the sickness is not his, she tells them where it came from (the hill lord's chest) without naming the man to them.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill spring, kanthal, the hill nymph and the velan's veri rite fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the falls, as music for the nymph's dance

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the god Murugan, named in line 11

35.reading: The day after the wedding, when the groom thanks her for keeping the girl well, the friend says that the girl's beauty, like that of Maranthai with its harbour, where on the long wave-beaten sandbank a bee takes the dark fruit of the naval for its kin and swarms on it, a crab takes the bee for fruit and seizes it, and the bee's buzz, like an untuned string, draws the prey-seeking heron, which lets them go, was always so, as he can see; but though he has not left her side, has her beauty slackened a little, or is it love, like the elation of toddy-drinkers, that has paled her eyes?
35.nuance: The chain of mistakes on the shore (bee taking fruit for kin, crab taking bee for fruit, heron letting all go) is a traditional site for hidden meaning, but no two of its parts map firmly onto the wedding situation, so it stays scene; the friend turns the groom's thanks back on him by giving the pallor to love rather than to her care.

colophon.thurai: மணமகனைப் பிற்றை ஞான்று புக்க தோழி நன்கு ஆற்றுவித்தாய் என்ற தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the wave-beaten sandbank, its crab and heron fix the shore

comparisons.tenor: the bee's buzzing
the girl's beauty
her love

36.reading: With the man listening at the night tryst, the friend says that, trusting the word of the hill lord, in whose land a short-legged tiger, strong to kill, strikes down a great tusker in a deep pool so that his flower-browed mate is left to grieve, they have lost their beauty, while the noisy town, joining the gossiping women's whispers at midnight and taking up their wicked talk, has made an endless scandal of it: what has the town itself lost?
36.nuance: The tiger could instead be the man, whose word has cost them their beauty; either way the scene of the killing and the lone mate is not joined to the speech by any marker.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger, the elephants and the hill lord fix kurinji

ullurai.tenor: the lovers parted by the town's slander

pairs.situation: the slandering town, which strikes at night
the girl left lonely and grieving

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses beasts of the hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

37.reading: The friend tells the man, who is leaving with the marriage put off, that it would be good if he took the sharp-toothed girl with him across the old wide wilds, where the tangled thickets have withered and a single cow's clear bell tinkles softly in a herd grazing on dry fodder; but if he leaves without love, so that her eyes like great water-girt blue lilies weep and she is distraught like a doe deserted by its stag, her grief will be more than the friend can bear when the rain-making evening comes, with the roaring thunder that strikes the dread heads of serpents as it wanders the sky.
37.nuance: The friend's threat is the rainy evening of mullai, the season of waiting, carried into a poem of the dry road: the danger she names is not the wilds but the evening at home.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's leaving across the dry wilds before marriage is pirithal

comparisons.tenor: her eyes
the girl, distraught when he leaves

38.reading: The girl answers her friend's reassurance: though their noisy town, Kaandavaayil, with its gardens ringed by the backwater, its fences of thorny palm-leaf over which the palmyra climbs and its white sands, is full of bustle and plenty, the catch never failing, the nets rich, the rains never failing, the fishermen bartering and drinkers merry on sweet palm toddy, it turns desolate if the lord of the shore with his chariot leaves her.
38.nuance: The prosperity is listed only to be cancelled: the whole loud town weighs less than one man's going, and the closing 'our noisy town' (அழுங்கல் ஊர்) is the same noise heard as loneliness.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, nets, palmyra and backwater fix the shore

39.reading: At their second meeting the man tells the girl that she does not answer his words and bows her lovely face in shame, yet when love overflows is it easy to hold back? her eyes, red at the corners like the tusk tips of an elephant reeking of flesh after a tiger has gored its dark back and toyed with it, are not angry, but her shoulders painted with sugarcane designs, like the great-named Koodal of Cheliyan who took the drums and crossed the guarded walls of foes, overpower him, bright goddess.
39.nuance: Both similes are of violence (the gored elephant's bloody tusk, the conqueror's city), turned on a shy girl who says nothing: the man reads his own defeat in her body, and calls her அணங்கு, a power that strikes.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger and the elephant of the hill and a meeting of the lovers fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the red corners of her eyes
her painted shoulders

40.reading: The other woman says, within hearing of the wife's attendants, that at the guarded house where the long-tongued bell rings, the sand-strewn pandal is roofed with leaves, great bards keep watch and decked women stand on one side seeking omens, while the boy sleeps on a soft bed under spread cloth beside a nurse smelling of new birth and the noble mother, bathed in ghee with white mustard, soft-bodied, has shut both eyes, the lord of the wide-ford town too came at midnight like a thief, because a son was born bearing his grandfather's name.
40.nuance: The 'too' (ஊரனும்) sets the husband among the other night visitors to a guarded house; the courtesan describes the birth-house rites in close detail, so her mockery shows she knows the household from outside.

thinai_evidence.note: the other woman's jibe at the husband's furtive visit to his own house is oodal

comparisons.tenor: the husband coming to his own house at midnight

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: she speaks to her own companions; the overhearers are the wife's attendants

links.note: Both are by Maruthan Ilanaganar on the same occasion (the man, his work done, speaks to his charioteer): in Akananuru 34 a stag feeds and guards his doe, in Natrinai 21 a forest cock scratches out its morning food and looks to its hen, and both close the image on the same word, பெருந்தகை / பெருந்தகு.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows one poet keeping a fixed frame for this thurai, a male creature's noble care for its mate seen from the speeding chariot, and changing only the creature, so the iraicchi of the homecoming was a reusable device rather than a chance sight.

links.note: Natrinai 23's friend says the girl's thinness is hidden by her bangles and her loose hair excused by play, but her eyes cannot hide love; Kural 1271 has the man tell her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say.
links.teaches: The Natrinai supplies the test behind Valluvar's claim by sorting the signs of love into those an excuse can cover and the eyes, which none can, so the couplet's 'though you hide' turns out to name a practice of concealment the older poem lays out part by part.

links.note: Both rest on the maxim that work is what men are: in Kuruntokai 135 the friend adds that men are the life of the women at home and concludes that he will put off going; in Natrinai 24 the woman adds nothing and praises her friend for consenting to his going. On the plain reading the two conclusions are incompatible.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the saying about men and work was common ground each speaker could turn either way, toward consenting to the parting or toward stopping it, so the maxim settled nothing and each poem's argument lies in what it adds to it.

links.note: Both are by Peri Saathanar and both name the man as the one who chased parrots from the millet with them (கிளி கடிந்து ... நம்மொடு; கிள்ளை நம்மொடு கடிந்தோன்): in Natrinai 25 he leaves without finding a chance to speak, and in Akananuru 242 the mother, not knowing this same man came in love, calls the velan.
links.teaches: Read together, the poet's one formula marks two stages of a single courtship, the silent visitor at the millet field whose plea the friend carries and the unseen cause of the sickness the mother misreads, so the parrot-chasing stranger is what separates the friend's knowledge from the mother's ignorance.

links.note: Natrinai 32's friend ends with the saying that the great take a friend after inquiry and do not inquire after befriending, and that once accepted it is hard to undo; Kural 791 says nothing brings ruin like befriending without inquiry, since there is no leaving once the bond is formed.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule and its reason, inquire first because a formed bond cannot be left, already serve in the Natrinai as a proverb a friend applies to a girl choosing a lover, so the ethics of friendship framed the irrevocability of a love match before Valluvar set them apart in his book on polity.

links.note: In Akananuru 242 the friend calls the velan ignorant (அறியா வேலன்) for finding Murugan's seizure in the girl; in Natrinai 34 the friend addresses Murugan himself, who knows the sickness is not his yet comes to the veri at the velan's call, and calls the god a fool.
links.teaches: Together they show the friend's scorn for the veri rite moving up from the priest to the god: where one poem blames only the diviner's ignorance, the other makes the god complicit, since he knows the truth and comes anyway.

links.note: Both liken a woman's beauty to Kuttuvan's harbour town Maranthai: in Akananuru 376 the deserted courtesan asks the man to give back her Maranthai-like beauty before he goes; in Natrinai 35 the friend, the day after the wedding, asks whether the wife's Maranthai-like beauty has slackened though he has not left her side.
links.teaches: The same city-simile measures a beauty the man must answer for in both, but the pair shows it waning for opposite reasons, the courtesan's because he left and the new wife's while he stays, so the Natrinai places the loss in love itself rather than in absence.

links.note: Purananuru 72 has Neduncheliyan vow to rout the kings who mocked him and seize them together with their drums (முரசமொடு); Natrinai 39 names Cheliyan as the one who took the drums and crossed the foes' guarded walls (முரசு கொண்டு ஓம்பு அரண் கடந்த) and likens the girl's shoulders to his Koodal. The Natrinai does not say which Cheliyan; the drum-taking matches.
links.teaches: The pair shows a king's battle vow hardened into a stock epithet inside a love simile and turned on the lover: the city of the king who took walled forts becomes the measure of shoulders that overpower the man, so puram conquest lends akam its language of love's assault.

source_issues: Natrinai colophons give speaker, addressee and occasion in prose; thurai_akam follows them, and where they name no addressee (29, 34, 40) the code is pira with a note.
23: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but the poem's only native things are of the Korkai shore (pearls, neythal) and its situation is the girl's grief; I infer neythal.
28: the colophon thinai is பாலை; the poem has only hill things (falls, vengai, bamboo) and no road, so I infer kurinji, keeping pirithal as the uri.
32: the colophon has the friend speak to the girl, but the poem addresses வாழி தோழி; the friend may be so addressed, so I keep the colophon's speaker.
40: the colophon's தலைமகட்குச் பாங்காயினார் has ச் before ப, apparently a misprint for தலைமகட்குப்.
22 line 10, 37 line 4, 40 line 6: the lost -ஒடு vowel sign restored (text flag); 32 line 4, 36 line 9, 39 line 10: tamilvu.org readings replace ours (text flag); 31 line 5 repeats as 311 line 7.
